cues.text: A Society Under Growing Attack
By the mid-eighteenth century, the Society of Jesus was wealthy, influential, and deeply embedded in Catholic Europe and its colonies.
It had accumulated powerful enemies among Enlightenment critics of Church influence, Jansenist rivals within the Church itself, and above all the absolutist monarchs of Catholic Europe.
These monarchs increasingly resented the Society's independence from royal control and its direct obedience to the pope.
Expelled Kingdom by Kingdom
Beginning with Portugal in 1759, followed by France in 1764 and Spain and its vast American empire in 1767, one Catholic monarchy after another expelled the Jesuits from its territories.
They seized the Jesuits’ considerable property and confiscated their schools and missions, often on fabricated or exaggerated charges of conspiracy and disloyalty.
The Bourbon courts of Spain, France, and Naples then jointly pressed the papacy itself to dissolve the order entirely.
Clement XIV's Decision
Under sustained and unrelenting political pressure from the Bourbon monarchies, Pope Clement XIV issued the brief Dominus ac Redemptor on July 21, 1773.
It suppressed the Society of Jesus throughout the Catholic world, dissolving its governing structure and releasing its members from their Jesuit vows.
The brief placed the Society’s considerable property and institutions under local episcopal control.

The pope's own private correspondence suggests he acted less from conviction that the Society had genuinely erred than from a judgment that its continued existence threatened a far more damaging rupture with the Bourbon courts.
Survival Under a Sympathetic Empress
The suppression was never fully enforced everywhere.
Catherine the Great of Russia, whose territory included formerly Polish lands with an active Jesuit presence, declined to promulgate the papal brief within her own dominions.

This allowed a small remnant of the Society to continue functioning legally in Russian territory throughout the decades of formal suppression elsewhere—an unlikely refuge for a Catholic religious order preserved by the deliberate choice of an Orthodox empress.
Legacy
The Society of Jesus remained suppressed for over four decades, its former members scattered into diocesan ministry or other communities.
Pope Pius VII , restored to Rome after the fall of Napoleon, formally revived the order worldwide in 1814 through the bull Sollicitudo Omnium Ecclesiarum .
This drew in part on the very Russian remnant that had quietly kept the Jesuit tradition of formation and governance alive throughout the long years of suppression elsewhere.
Within a generation, the Society resumed much of the missionary and educational work for which it had once been suppressed.
